improvement_notes: Clarify that the recursive program uses a path-local visited set with backtracking; this is different from a globally visited set used by some graph-search algorithms.
Replace the loose cycle definition with a more precise explanation: a cycle is a closed sequence of edges that returns to an earlier node. Distinguish cycles from repeated-node walks.
The section instructing an illustrator to create a warehouse map is redundant after the lesson already presents generated visuals. Convert it into a student diagram activity or remove it.
Add a short sample output block for the Python lab so students can verify not only the assertions but also the four discovered routes and their costs.
In the optional travel-time extension, explicitly state that every edge incident to Ramp is affected by the slower speed and demonstrate one complete conversion, such as 4 m at 0.5 m/s = 8 s.

The generated engineering schematic is described generically as a left-to-right signal diagram, while the lesson's central visual need is graph structure. Add a caption-specific reading guide that names the graph, route, cost, and sensor elements.
The lesson could briefly distinguish a simple path from a general walk before introducing the code, reducing possible confusion around route repetition and cycle handling.
Consider adding one short question about whether the listed graph is truly undirected and why each reverse connection is present in the Python representation.

linkedin.title: Graph Search for Robotics: Modeling Routes, Costs, and Real-World Constraints
linkedin.description: A practical Professor OS lesson introduces nodes, edges, path costs, route comparison, recursive search, and the gap between a warehouse graph and physical robot reality.
linkedin.commentary:
A robot cannot plan a route until its environment has been represented in a form a computer can search.

Professor OS Class 38 introduces graph search through a warehouse navigation problem built around RoboRover:

• Model meaningful locations as nodes and possible movements as edges.
• Add costs for distance, time, energy, or risk.
• Compare complete route costs instead of choosing the cheapest immediate move.
• Use a small Python search to enumerate simple routes and verify the best result.
• Examine why sensors must validate a graph that may no longer match the real warehouse.

The lesson combines equations, a worked example, an interactive route-design activity, and executable code. Students also modify the graph by adding a cold-storage area and explore how changing the meaning of cost can change planning decisions.

Try the paper-based RoboRover Route Captain activity, then run the code and predict its output before executing it.
